summary: Clarifies the definition of a secured zone in DNSSEC, updating RFC 2535 so a zone is secured or not regardless of the key algorithm used. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

eli5.summary: A zone is either locked or not locked, no matter how many kinds of lock exist. Newer documents later replaced this.

questions: what is a secured dns zone
dnssec zone status globally secured locally secured
subtitle: How to define whether a DNS zone is secured by DNSSEC.

tldr.problem: RFC 2535 defined DNSSEC security per algorithm, so a zone could be secured with one algorithm but not another. This created confusion and complexity for implementers and operators.
tldr.mechanism: This document simplifies the definition: a zone is either secured or not secured, regardless of algorithm. It defines three levels: globally secured (follows standard chain of trust), locally secured (uses non-standard validation), and unsecured.
tldr.outcome: Zone status is clearer and easier to determine. The document was superseded by RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035.

today: RFC 3090 has been superseded by RFC 4033, RFC 4034, and RFC 4035, which provide updated DNSSEC protocol specifications. Current DNSSEC implementations should follow these newer RFCs.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) use digital signatures to verify DNS data. A critical question for DNS administrators, servers, and resolvers is: Is this zone secured? Zone administrators need to know what steps to take to secure a zone. Dynamic update servers need to know whether to apply DNSSEC processing. Parent zones need to indicate whether child zones are secured. Resolvers need to know whether to expect valid signatures.

RFC 2535 originally defined zone security on a per-algorithm basis: a zone could be secured with RSA keys but unsecured for DSA keys. This granular approach proved confusing in practice. RFC 3090 simplifies this by defining a zone as simply secured or unsecured, regardless of algorithm choice.

The document also deprecates the concept of experimentally secure zones, which were intended to facilitate migration but created additional complexity. A zone administrator can achieve the same goal more simply using locally secured status.
sections.eli5: Early DNSSEC rules had different security levels depending on the type of lock used. This simplifies it: a zone is locked or unlocked, period.

sections.title: Globally and Locally Secured Zones
sections.content:
A globally secured zone follows the strictest DNSSEC rules. It uses only mandatory-to-implement algorithms (per RFC 2535 section 3.2) and relies on a chain of trust that parallels the DNS delegation tree — meaning each zone's keys are signed by its parent zone, all the way up to a trusted root.

For a zone to be globally secured, it must have at least one zone signing KEY record at its apex using a mandatory algorithm, signed by the parent zone. The parent's signing key must also be a zone signing KEY using a mandatory algorithm. The zone must deploy NXT (Next) records throughout to provide complete denial of existence. Every record set must be signed by one of the zone's mandatory-algorithm keys.

A locally secured zone is similar but allows deviations: the signing algorithm need not be mandatory-to-implement, and the chain of trust can rely on off-tree validation (such as a trusted third party or pre-configuration in resolvers) rather than the parent zone. Locally secured zones still require NXT records and proper signatures, but can use non-standard algorithms or validation paths.

The document introduces the concept of islands of security — contiguous groups of secured zones surrounded by unsecured zones. A locally secured zone is often the root of such an island.
sections.eli5: A zone can be locked in the standard way (parent vouches for child all the way up to the root) or in a custom way (some other authority approves it). Either way, it's locked.

sections.title: Security Roots and Chain of Trust
sections.content:
Every secured zone must have a security context: a starting point from which trust flows. For globally secured zones, the security chain is on-tree — it parallels the DNS delegation hierarchy. Resolvers verify zone keys by tracing upward through parent signatures until reaching a trusted root.

For locally secured zones, the security chain is off-tree — it can use authorities outside the standard hierarchy. This includes certification authorities that sign zone keys, pre-configured keys in resolvers, or other trusted parties.

The document defines the closest security root as the security root with the most matching labels when descending toward a given domain. This helps disambiguate when multiple islands of security exist. For example, if both "exp.test." and "testing.signed.exp.test." are security roots and you are verifying "sub.domain.testing.signed.exp.test.", the latter is closest (4 matching labels vs. 2).

Islands of security can overlap but the definition ensures resolvers examine the correct verification chain. Parent zones indicate to child zones whether the child is secured by stating it explicitly (via a KEY record) or implying it through the absence of such a statement.
sections.eli5: To verify a locked zone, you follow the signature chain upward to a key you trust. That starting key is the security root.

sections.title: Unsecured Zones and Experimental Status Deprecation
sections.content:
An unsecured zone is any zone that does not meet the criteria for globally or locally secured status. This includes zones with no signatures, incomplete NXT record coverage, or signatures using non-mandatory algorithms without off-tree validation support.

RFC 2535 defined an experimentally secure status to facilitate migration from unsecured to secured zones. A zone could publish signatures and be tested before wide deployment. However, this status created unnecessary complexity. RFC 3090 deprecates it, allowing the same functionality via locally secured status: a zone administrator can publish signatures and configure test resolvers with the zone's public keys, achieving the same goal without a special designation.

This simplification reduces the number of security states resolvers must handle from four (globally secured, locally secured, experimentally secured, unsecured) to three (globally secured, locally secured, unsecured).
sections.eli5: Zones that aren't locked properly are unsecured. The old "experimental" lock status is removed; zones can test security privately without a special label.

sections.title: Determining Zone Status in Practice
sections.content:
The document provides rules for determining whether a zone is secured in various contexts. When a zone administrator configures a zone, they determine status by examining its KEY records, signatures and NXT records against the criteria for global or local security.

A dynamic update server determines zone status similarly, examining zone data to decide whether to apply DNSSEC processing. A parent zone indicates child zone status through presence or absence of KEY records (silence means secured; an explicit unsigned KEY record with NULL algorithm means unsecured).

Resolvers follow the most restrictive rules when verifying data. A resolver that only supports mandatory-to-implement algorithms will only see globally secured zones as secured. A resolver supporting additional algorithms may see locally secured zones as secured. The designations "globally" and "locally" are not standards-compliance states but simply identify the attributes and scope of a zone's security.

The document emphasizes that declaring a zone "completely" secured is impossible — misbehaving resolvers or non-compliant parents can subvert security. The best achievable state is that all parties comply with the rules and security incidents can be traced quickly.
sections.eli5: To know if a zone is locked, examine its records and signatures. Different resolvers might see it differently depending on how strict they are.
